name: Orthodontic headgear / facemask

lead: Headgear and facemasks apply outside-the-mouth force to guide jaw growth and correct bites in children, with the facemask pulling the upper jaw forward for underbites.
Trials support use in growing patients. Looksmaxxing claims of forward maxillary growth in adults are not backed by the sources reviewed.

paras: Straps anchor to the head or neck, and elastics or a frame transmit force to the teeth and jaw, restraining or advancing the upper jaw.
Eye injuries, tooth soreness, social stigma and possible airway or facial-growth effects are reported; effectiveness depends on many hours of daily wear.

lead: Orthodontic headgear is an appliance worn partly outside the mouth, anchored by straps to the head or neck, that applies force to the teeth or jaws to correct the bite and guide growth, mainly in children [1]. A reverse-pull headgear or facemask rests on the forehead and chin and uses elastics to pull the upper jaw forward, and is used for underbites [1][2].

The Cochrane review of orthodontic treatment for Class III malocclusion in children describes the facemask as the most commonly reported non-surgical intervention, usually attached to an expansion appliance [2]. In looksmaxxing communities, facemasks combined with MARPE are discussed as a non-surgical route to forward maxillary growth, a claim for which published support concerns children rather than adults.
infobox: Facebow headgear, cervical headgear, reverse-pull facemask [1]
Commonly 12 to 23 hours a day; 14 to 16 often prescribed [1]
Eye injuries reported; safety release designs exist [1]

paras: Standard facebow headgear attaches to molar tubes and mainly pulls the upper molars back or restrains upper jaw growth; cervical and helmet versions anchor around the neck or head; the reverse-pull facemask pulls the upper jaw forward [1]. Purposes include correcting protruding upper teeth, treating underbites and making space for crowded teeth [1].

A randomised two-phase trial of early Class II treatment reported favourable growth changes in about 75% of children treated early with a headgear or a functional appliance [3]. The Cochrane review covers facemask treatment of Class III malocclusion in children [2]. A 1981 study examined orthodontic cooperation, including headgear wear, using psychological measures [4], and a review of temporary anchorage devices notes that extraoral headgear suffers from compliance problems [5].

Wikipedia reports that long-term studies suggest headgear may flatten the face, restrict chin growth and reduce airway size, that eye injuries have occurred, and that tooth soreness and social stigma are common [1]. Safety facebows and release straps reduce injury risk [1].

looksmax.org threads discuss MARPE with a facemask for a recessed maxilla [6], expected forward growth in adults [7], and whether such expansion works at all [8]. One thread asks about growth-hormone and other compounds to accompany treatment [9]; no published study in the sources reviewed supports such combinations. Responses vary, with some posters telling a user in his late teens that results would be negligible at that age [6].

Trials and reviews concern children: the Class II headgear trial [3], the Class III facemask Cochrane review [2], and compliance research [4][5]. No studies found of facemask treatment for aesthetic purposes in adults.

lore.intro: Headgear and facemasks are discussed on looksmax.org as a non-surgical way to advance a recessed maxilla.
